piOfficeOld: My own office. Every decision is mine. So is every consequence.
A small practice. Ideally, the practice will make me better at it.
No department to transfer the call to. I have checked.
There is something reassuring about a workplace where I know who moved my things. Usually me.
I should check the classifieds. Clients rarely introduce themselves as a sustainable business model.
Being self-employed means I can choose which problem to worry about first.
A modest headquarters. The mysteries will have to be impressed by the service.
I can call it a private practice. "One person with a telephone" sounds less established.
A small office encourages focus. There are fewer places to avoid the work.
I should keep the cases separate. "A suspicious person" is not a filing category.
There is no supervisor here. I shall have to provide my own disappointed silence.
The business needs a reputation. Preferably one I do not have to explain.

computer: The computer. Receptionist, noticeboard, and the only colleague I can restart.
Classified ads. Somewhere between the ordinary requests is an extraordinary amount of trouble.
I should read what the client actually wants before deciding what I can promise.
An inbox is not a business plan. It is, however, a place to start.
The office shop is dangerously close to the work I opened the computer to do.
The computer stores my cases. I remain responsible for not confusing them.
phone: My business line. I should sound like a detective, not someone surprised to receive a call.
A telephone turns a promising theory into a question somebody can refuse to answer.
I should have the name ready before I dial. "You know, the suspicious one" rarely helps.
One receiver. Several possible versions of the truth.
An incoming call could be work. An outgoing call could establish whether I understand the work.
I should listen for what they say, not what would improve the case.
cityDoor: The city is outside. The investigation is unlikely to deliver itself.
I should know where I am going before making an impressive exit.
A private office is useful. Private investigations occasionally require leaving it.
Out there, people have answers. They also have their own ideas about sharing them.
Best take a clear question into the city. It is large enough without a vague one.
I can investigate the neighbourhood, or continue establishing that I own a door.

noCase: No active job. I should look through the classifieds instead of waiting for a dramatic knock.
An empty caseload. Good for organisation, less convincing as a profession.
I have room for a client. Physically and professionally.
Time to read the adverts carefully. The shortest request is not always the simplest.
caseAccepted: A new client request. I should record what was agreed before the story starts growing.
Job accepted. First, separate the request from my assumptions about it.
I have a case. The office is now a headquarters rather than an expensive place to sit.
A client has trusted me with a problem. Best return something more useful than confidence.
caseCompleted: One job finished. I should keep the notes; my next brilliant idea may be something I already checked.
That case is complete. A useful reminder that asking the right questions works.
A finished job. I should review the correspondence before answering anything else.
Case completed. I shall allow myself one professional nod.
computerLowCash: I should compare the price with my own cash, not with how successful the furniture makes me feel.
The shop has excellent suggestions. My wallet has submitted a shorter list.
I need to earn the next improvement before admiring it as a business necessity.
A new office would be nice. Having money after buying it would also have its uses.
